title: The Untold Influence of Joanna (Luke 8:3)
paragraphs: The Untold Influence of Joanna (Luke 8:3)
She moved in the halls of power.
But her money followed a rejected Messiah.

Joanna gets one line in Luke 8:3. One line. And most people scroll right past her. But that single verse carries a thunderclap: she was “the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager”… and she helped support Jesus and the disciples out of her own means.
Feel that tension.

A woman connected to Herod’s court—the same political world dripping with compromise, intimidation, and blood—quietly becomes a partner in the ministry of Christ. Not from a platform. Not from a pulpit. From hidden faithfulness. From surrendered resources. From a heart that decided Jesus was worth more than status.
And that is where many miss the power of Joanna.

She proves that influence is not measured by how loud your name is. Influence is measured by what your life is financing, serving, and advancing. Some people use access to build themselves. Joanna used access to bless the kingdom. She took what could have been a life of comfort and turned it into an offering.
Think about it.
While others were trying to silence Jesus, Joanna was helping sustain the mission.
While men argued about greatness, Joanna was already pouring her substance into the Gospel.
While religious pride wanted front-row honor, this woman was using what she had so the Son of God could keep moving from town to town, preaching good news to the poor.
And she didn’t disappear after that.

In Luke 24:10, Joanna appears again among the women who testified about the empty tomb. She was there in the ministry. She was there in the resurrection story. Hidden in the text, but never hidden from God.
That preaches.
Because heaven remembers the names earth forgets.

Maybe you are not the one holding the microphone. Maybe your role feels unseen. Maybe your obedience is quiet, costly, and buried under somebody else’s spotlight. Hear me: Jesus sees Joanna people. The ones who give. The ones who open doors. The ones who sustain ministry. The ones whose faithfulness makes Gospel movement possible.
But here’s the deeper wound.

Our hearts love visible influence because our flesh wants credit. We want applause, control, recognition. Yet the kingdom of God is built by crucified people—people who lay down pride, possessions, and reputation at the feet of Christ. Joanna’s story is beautiful not because she was connected, but because she surrendered her connection to something greater.
That is the Gospel.

Jesus does not save us so we can polish our image. He saves us so everything we are—our story, our scars, our access, our resources, our influence—can be placed under His lordship. Sin curves us inward. Grace turns us outward. And at the center stands Christ, who gave not part of Himself, but all of Himself on the cross for sinners like us. Then He rose, and now even the overlooked can become vessels of eternal impact.
So no, Joanna is not a footnote.
She is a witness.

A warning to the proud.
A comfort to the unseen.
A call to every believer: Put your influence in the hands of Jesus.
Because when Christ takes hold of a life, even one verse can carry a legacy.
